Madhav: did you do your two-minute check?
Yogesh: yes. name spelled right, company name right (I'd typed the wrong one!), CV attached, right file, deadline date, and I reread what they asked for
Yogesh: takes two minutes, I keep the list on a sticky note
Madhav: that list is why mistakes get caught

qa.q: What might Yogesh be feeling on sending at 4:52?

qa.q: What would you advise Yogesh to do next time?
qa.a: Start the check earlier so there is room to fix things without racing the deadline.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Yogesh's checklist habit?

passage: At the cyber cafe near the bus stand in a small town, Kashish had the scholarship form ready to send. Leela, who ran the cafe, saw the hesitation over the button. "Do your check first," Leela said, and slid a list from the desk drawer: name as on the ID, date of birth, marks, phone number, photo, right document attached, and what the notice had asked for. Kashish went down it with a finger. The phone number had one digit swapped. The marksheet attached was the front page only. She fixed both and pressed submit, and the receipt printed. "Two minutes," Leela said. "That saves you a trip and a rejection."

qa.q: What two errors did Kashish find on the list?
qa.a: A swapped digit in the phone number, and a marksheet with only the front page attached.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling while hesitating over the button?
qa.a: Nervous and unsure, not certain that everything on the form was right.

qa.q: How did the list help?
qa.a: It made Kashish check one item at a time, catching two errors before submitting.

qa.q: Why might Leela keep the checklist in the drawer?
qa.a: Leela has probably seen many errors from customers and wants to prevent repeat trips and rejections.

grounding: Shows a careful person using a short checklist to catch small errors before submitting a form.

passage:
In Hanoi, Bao had twenty minutes left before the scholarship portal closed. His friend Yosef, visiting from Tel Aviv, watched from the sofa as Bao's finger hovered over "Submit."
Bao stopped. He peeled a yellow sticky note off his monitor. On it were four lines: Names spelled right? Numbers match? Attachments right files? Answered what they asked?
Names: his own, his referee's. Fine. Numbers: his grade average matched the transcript. Fine. Attachments: he opened each one. The second file was his CV from two years ago. His face went hot. He swapped it. The original request: the essay asked for "a challenge you overcame," and he had written about a success. He added one paragraph.
Two minutes, then one more read. He clicked submit with four minutes left.
Yosef laughed. "You check like a pilot."
Bao grinned, though his hands were still a bit cold. "Better than finding out afterwards."

qa.q: Which file had Bao attached wrongly?
qa.a: The second file was his CV from two years ago.

qa.q: How did Bao feel when he found the old CV?
qa.a: Bao felt embarrassed and alarmed; his face went hot, though he was relieved to catch it in time.

qa.q: Which part of Bao's checklist saved him, and why?
qa.a: Opening each attachment, because it caught the old CV that he would never have noticed from the file name.

qa.q: How does Yosef see Bao's checking?
qa.a: Yosef finds it impressive and a little funny, saying Bao checks like a pilot.

grounding: Illustrates a careful person who runs a short checklist on names, numbers, attachments and the original request before submitting.

passage:
In the college admin office, Gopika, a second-year student doing a work-study job, had drafted the circular about the exam timetable. Parul, the office supervisor, was waiting to send it to all eight hundred students.
"Two minutes," Gopika said, and pulled up the checklist she had pinned above her desk after her first week. Names: the course codes matched the department list. Numbers: dates and rooms. She checked them against the master timetable, line by line. Chemistry was on the 14th in her draft; the master said the 16th.
She fixed it. Attachments: the seating plan PDF. She opened it. It was right. Original request: Parul had asked for the timetable and the rule about calculators. The calculator rule was missing. She added it.
She sent it to Parul, who read it and nodded. "Last year, someone sent the wrong date to everyone. We had forty students at the wrong exam."
Gopika let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

qa.q: What date did the master timetable give for Chemistry?
qa.a: The master said the 16th.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel when Parul mentioned last year's wrong date?
qa.a: Gopika felt a rush of relief, letting out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

qa.q: What two errors did the checklist catch, and why does that matter?
qa.a: The wrong Chemistry date and the missing calculator rule, which would otherwise have gone to eight hundred students.

qa.q: How might Parul see Gopika's two-minute check?
qa.a: Parul seems reassured and approving, remembering the chaos of last year's wrong date.

grounding: Shows a careful student worker who uses a short checklist before sending, catching a wrong date and a missing request.

passage:
Dear Yogesh,
You start sending job applications this week, so I'm going to tell you my most embarrassing story, and then give you my checklist.
Two years ago, I sent a cover letter to a design firm addressed to "Dear Hiring Team at Silverline." The firm was called Northgate. Silverline was the previous application. I found out when their HR replied, very politely, pointing it out. I wanted to hide under my desk for a week.
Since then, before I send anything important, I spend two minutes on four checks:
1. Names: company, person, my own.
2. Numbers: dates, phone number, any figures.
3. Attachments: open every one, don't trust the file name.
4. The original request: reread what they asked for and see if I answered it.
It has caught something almost every time. Last month it caught a salary figure with an extra zero.
Two minutes. Please.
Your sister,
Minakshi

qa.q: What was the firm Minakshi applied to actually called?
qa.a: The firm was called Northgate.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when the HR reply came?
qa.a: Minakshi felt deeply embarrassed, wanting to hide under the desk for a week.

qa.q: Which of the four checks might matter most for Yogesh, and why?
qa.a: Checking names, because sending a letter with another company's name is the kind of embarrassing error a two-minute check catches.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel reading this?
qa.a: Yogesh would probably feel amused by the story but also grateful, since it gives a simple habit before those first applications.

grounding: Illustrates a careful person who, after an embarrassing error, uses a short checklist of names, numbers, attachments and the original request.

passage:
Mohit, before you hit submit on that internship application, let me tell you about my checklist. In first year I emailed a cover letter to a firm in Chennai that began "Dear Hiring Team at" followed by the name of a totally different company. I'd copied it from my previous application. They never replied. I didn't blame them.
So now I, Naveen, never send anything important without four checks. One: every name. Is it theirs, spelt right? Two: every number: dates, marks, phone. Three: attachments. Actually attached, and the right version, not "CV_old". Four: I reopen their original message and tick off everything they asked for. Takes two minutes, maybe three.
Last month it caught a wrong date on my scholarship form and a missing transcript. Nobody saw those mistakes except me, and that's the whole point. Okay, now open yours and read me their original email.

qa.q: Which four things does Naveen check before sending?
qa.a: Every name, every number, the attachments, and the original message's list of what they asked for.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the first-year cover letter?
qa.a: Naveen felt embarrassed and didn't blame the firm for not replying, since the letter named a totally different company.

qa.q: What could Mohit do right now, before submitting?
qa.a: Mohit could reopen the internship's original email and tick off each item, then check the names, numbers and that the right attachments are there.

qa.q: How might the firm in Chennai have seen Naveen's letter?
qa.a: They probably saw it as careless copying, since it opened with another company's name, and simply didn't reply.

grounding: Shows a careful person using a short checklist of names, numbers, attachments and the original request before submitting.
